articles.title_orig: Mamdani defends Oct. 7 message that angered Jewish leaders, unnerved some Democrats
articles.title_zh: Mamdani defends Oct. 7 message that angered Jewish leaders, unnerved some Democrats
articles.content_orig:
UNION SQUARE, Manhattan (WABC) -- Mayor Zohran Mamdani defended his Oct. 7 statement on Thursday after facing criticism from some members of the city's Jewish community over remarks that referenced both Israelis killed in the Oct. 7 attacks and Palestinians killed in Gaza.
Mamdani appeared at a news conference in Bushwick on grants to nonprofits Thursday morning, less than 12 hours after demonstrators interrupted a vigil in Union Square for the hundreds of Israelis killed on Oct. 7.
The mayor was escorted past angry pro-Palestinian demonstrators at the vigil as chants echoed through the streets, with some calling him a "traitor."
In a statement issued Wednesday, Mamdani said:
"We grieve alongside our many friends and neighbors who still carry that unthinkable loss. The suffering did not begin nor end that day. It instead continued through the Israeli government's devastating, ongoing genocide in Gaza. Many New Yorkers are reckoning with this unbearable grief, and we mourn alongside them - all while knowing that our tax dollars fund these war crimes."
Speaking Thursday, Mamdani said he stood by those remarks and rejected suggestions that he should apologize.
"It is critically important to be able to mourn for all of those who were killed—and have been killed since. Especially given that we know this is ongoing, as opposed to something simply that was three years ago," he said.
The mayor's reference to the Israeli military response to Oct. 7 in a statement marking the anniversary drew criticism from some in the city's Jewish community. Mamdani defended his position Thursday.
"We need not choose between which death we will mourn and which we will ignore, that we will reckon with the fact that all of it is to be opposed," he said.
City Council Speaker Julie Menin said she disagreed with the mayor's approach.
"I believe October 7th should focus on the events of October 7th, not on the aftermath, but on the events of October 7th—just as I believe on September 11th, we should focus on the events of September 11th, and that's where I put my focus," she said.
The exchange highlighted differing views among city leaders over how Oct. 7 should be commemorated and discussed.

articles.title_orig: Fiery Senate Debates in Maine, Michigan and Georgia: Five Takeaways
articles.title_zh: Fiery Senate Debates in Maine, Michigan and Georgia: Five Takeaways
articles.content_orig:
Candidates traded personal attacks and clashed over a range of issues in closely watched US Senate debates on Thursday, with control of Congress at stake
With just weeks left in the contentious midterm election campaign, candidates in a trio of highly-competitive Senate races debated Thursday night, clashing over the economy, tariffs, the Iran war and abortion rights, with control of the upper chamber at stake.
In Georgia, incumbent Democratic senator Jon Ossoff faced GOP representative Mike Collins. In Michigan, Democrat Abdul Al-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers debated over the state’s open Senate seat. And in Maine, longtime senator Susan Collins met Democratic challenger Troy Jackson. Democrats need to flip four Republican-held Senate seats to win the majority.
Here are the key takeaways from the battleground state debates.
Affordability was a major topic across all three debates on Thursday night, as voters consistently name the cost of goods, gas, housing and healthcare as their top concerns in this year’s midterms.
“Can you afford your gas? Can you afford your groceries under this guy who’s going to rubber stamp everything Donald Trump tells him to rubber stamp?” El-Sayed asked during the Michigan debate, the first of two in one of this cycle’s most fiercely contested races.
Both Rogers and El-Sayed said they support suspending a fuel tax to alleviate costs, while El-Sayed argued that the Iran war, which was driving up gas prices, needs to end. El-Sayed attacked Rogers for growing his personal wealth while in office as a US representative.
Rogers called El-Sayed “bought off” by billionaire George Soros, Hamas and Hezbollah. “We cannot afford Abdul, and we cannot risk his ideology,” Rogers said.
In Georgia, Ossoff repeatedly asked Collins to justify his support for Trump’s global tariff policies, which the senator said have “crushed Georgia families” and “strangled” economic growth.
“Let’s see if he has the courage to explain his votes,” Ossoff said, adding later: “Still have not heard an explanation for the tariffs.”
Collins, who is trying to cut into Ossoff’s lead, blamed inflation on Biden administration policies, singling out spending measures that his opponent had supported.
Later in Maine, where polls show a tight race, Jackson focused his remarks on pocketbook issues, including the sharp spike in heating oil costs and high energy prices.
Collins defended her record and argued that Maine had benefited from the $50bn rural health transformation fund that was appended to Trump’s signature tax cut and spending bill, the so-called Big Beautiful bill.
In the Georgia debate, a question about data centers erupted into a pointed, personal exchange between Ossoff and Collins.
“Mike Collins voted to take that money out of your pocket and out of your community and give it instead to data center developers,” Ossoff said.
He then accused Collins of being a “bigot” who has “hired half the Third Reich” – a reference to the congressman’s history of employing staffers who have expressed white nationalist, antisemitic, and extremist views online.
“If John Lewis were marching today from Selma to Montgomery,” Ossoff said of the late civil rights icon and long-serving Georgia congressman, “Mike Collins would be grabbing a billy club. His office has been in cahoots with some of the most notorious white supremacists on the country.”
Collins was asked directly about his son-in-law’s social media posts promoting white nationalist and antisemitic views.
“You know, Rick, that’s my family,” Collins replied. “That’s the craziness that Jon Ossoff has been spewing out there.” Collins noted that a New York man had recently been charged after threatening to kill him, and added: “I’ve condemned racism, antisemitism, hate; I don’t care where the source is. And I tell him that too, it’s wrong. We have no place in this world for that.”
Collins, meanwhile, sought to cast Ossoff as “radical” and an “extremist” whose record in the Senate had left the state “less safe, more expensive and worse off”.
Tariffs were also a topic of heated debate in Michigan, which shares hundreds of miles of border with Canada.
This week, Rogers publicly backtracked on previous support for Trump’s tariffs on the US’s northern neighbor , saying in a campaign ad that “Canada is not our enemy” and that the “tariff war” needed to end now.
During Thursday night’s debate, Rogers said he had spoken to the commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, this week to advocate for a deal between the two countries. There are tariffs in place that are “too high and not helpful for us”, Rogers said.
El-Sayed said he supports targeted, logical tariffs that protect Michigan manufacturing, but nothing like the “ham-fisted, chaotic, self-serving” tariffs Trump put in place. He called out Rogers for “flip-flopping” on the issue, saying he was only reversing his stance because of “sagging poll numbers”.
“He’s doing an ad drinking a Labatt and talking about the Red Wings, pretending like he was not for this the entire time,” El-Sayed said. “Be serious, my guy.”
In Maine, discussions about gas prices and the war in Iran raised notable tension in the second debate between Jackson and Collins, who is seeking a sixth term in her seat. “She’s the Chairman of Appropriations,” Jackson said. “Money has to come through them for these wars – she still can do something.”
Collins, who plans to continue leading the Appropriations committee if re-elected, said she had repeatedly supported war powers resolutions to halt Trump’s military action in Iran.
But Jackson pushed further, accusing the senator and her husband of profiting from the war.
She could use her leverage to stop this war, but instead they’re making money,” he said, prompting a furious response from Collins, who called the allegation “absolutely outrageous”.
“You owe me an apology,” she said.
In Maine, both candidates were also pressed to address inconsistencies in their positions on reproductive rights, a crucial issue for voters in the state.
“Our records have changed,” Jackson said. “Mine has gotten better – hers has gotten worse.”
He pointed to Collins’ vote to confirm supreme court justice Brett Kavanaugh, who helped overturn Roe v Wade in 2022 . Collins, one of just two Republican senators who supports abortion rights, has said she does not regret her vote for Kavanaugh, even though she believed he had given her private assurances before his 2018 confirmation that he would not overturn the landmark ruling. Collins sought to turn the issue back on her opponent, noting his past stances on abortion that have left many voters wary. “From 2000 until he ran for the house seat in 2013 was very anti-choice,” she said, accusing Jackson of having held “extremist” views on abortion. “He was for a bill that would not allow abortion when the mother’s life was at risk.” She also pointed to legislation she helped write that sought to “codify Roe v Wade nationwide,” but the bill never made it passed the Senate.
In Michigan, Rogers repeatedly attacked El-Sayed by attempting to tie him to Muslim terrorist groups, including Hamas, and suggested government surveillance would only bother someone if he or his family had something to hide.
Rogers brought up El-Sayed’s mom and sister, prompting El-Sayed to say at one point that Rogers should just come out and say what he’s been dancing around all night, after Rogers’ repeated references to terrorist groups.
“He wants this to be about anything but his own record,” El-Sayed said.
Rogers claimed El-Sayed refused to condemn a terrorist attack in Michigan earlier this year and the 7 October Hamas terrorist attacks in Gaza, although El-Sayed said he had condemned both.
But, El-Sayed added: “I’m not somebody who tries to make political theater out of other people’s pain.”
He also retorted to Rogers: “Did you sell your yachts?” Rogers responded: “I never owned a yacht in Florida, brother.”

October 8, 2026 at 11:47 pm
The season’s winningest driver adds another to his tally with a strong performance in Ohio
Michael “Buddy” Kofoid hit the entire field with a knockout punch Thursday night.
The World of Outlaws NOS Energy Drink Sprint Car Series rolled into Findlay, OH’s Millstream Speedway to kickoff Sheldon Haudenschild ’s NOS Energy Drink Buckeye Brawl Weekend . A stout field of 39 cars checked in, and Kofoid put a beatdown on them all in the Roth Motorsports No. 83.
The Penngrove, CA native rocketed out to the early advantage after starting on the pole for the 30-lapper. David Gravel settled into second and began to regain some ground on Kofoid as lapped traffic became a factor.
But late caution flags continued to clear the path ahead for Kofoid by giving him clean air. Garet Williamson ripped by Gravel late for second, but he also couldn’t pose a threat to Kofoid as the laps faded away. Kofoid took the checkered flag with more than a second advantage to claim round one of the three-round brawl.
“That whole race I could keep the car wherever I wanted it to be,” Kofoid said. “If I needed to pull out of line, I could do something good with it. It’s just a testament to how talented Dylan (Buswell) is as well as Nate (Knotts), and Peyton (Friedrich). They do an extremely good job. I’m very thankful to have them in my corner.”
Kofoid added to his Series-leading win total in 2026 with his 15th of the campaign. That also moved he and the Roth Motorsports crew one checkered flag away from making team history. If they can pick up one more before the season is over, they’ll equal the winningest World of Outlaws campaign in the long history of Dennis and Teresa’s famed team. The 24-year-old took sole possession of 23rd on the all-time win list with his 37th career score.
Garet Williamson finishes runner-up in the Fischer Motorsports No. 23 to get back on the podium for the first time in roughly a month, his 11th top three of the year.
David Gravel posted yet another solid finish with a third-place effort aboard the Big Game Motorsports No. 2. That’s 30 podiums in 2026 for the two-time and defending champion.
Spencer Bayston and Parker Price-Miller rounded out the top five.

The 10-year US Treasury yield was 5.22 per cent on Thursday, compared with 1.69 per cent for Chinese government bonds on their first trading day after the National Day holiday – a gap of about 3.5 percentage points, compared with a record 3.7 percentage points on September 9.
Jiang Zhenlong, an associate research fellow at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences’ Institute of Finance and Banking, argued that higher US yields weaken the appeal of yuan assets and add pressure on the exchange rate and capital flows, but also raise dollar funding costs.

articles.title_orig: Awa seeks one term in Congress: ‘I don’t care’ about world policies
articles.title_zh: Awa seeks one term in Congress: ‘I don’t care’ about world policies
articles.content_orig:
HONOLULU (HawaiiNewsNow) - Hawaii News Now interviewed U.S. Rep. Jill Tokuda and state Sen. Brenton Awa, candidates for Hawaii’s 2nd Congressional District, about the Iran war, aid to Israel and immigration enforcement.
Awa said he is seeking only one term in Congress.
“I only want to go for two years, one term, and the reason is, is because I don’t care about all of those world policies and all the votes that’ll have to be taken. I’ll have to care when I am taking it,” Awa said.
Awa said he wants money spent on the Iran war and support for Israel to instead go to American families dealing with disaster.
“But my biggest focus, if we’re going to send billions of dollars to Israel or another country, my only concern is why isn’t that money coming to Hawaii,” Awa said.
Tokuda said ending the war is the best way to reduce energy costs. She opposes aid to Israel because of its treatment of Palestinians.
“It’s a genocide,” Tokuda said.
“When you take a look at the weapons they are using, it was our weapons, which is why I voted against funding weapons sales to Israel for now, because that is blood on our hands,” Tokuda said.
On immigration enforcement, Awa does not oppose mass deportation but said he believes ICE has been too violent.
“The idea is good. The way they go and carry it out, and I don’t know,” Awa said. “I’m not there on the ground, so I don’t know, but other than what I see, through you guys, the media. But when you see people dying, there is no way that that should ever happen.”
Tokuda said there will be pressure to fix immigration laws after the election.
“We absolutely have to pass some kind of meaningful bipartisan immigration reform that protects our borders, that creates legal pathways to citizenship and doesn’t result in Americans getting executed in our streets,” Tokuda said.
Awa acknowledges the odds are stacked against him in a district that has never elected a Republican, and GOP voters have been discouraged by President Trump’s unpopularity.
Awa did not have to give up his Senate seat to run for Congress and has two years remaining on his term.

articles.title_orig: The advice immigration attorneys have for Microsoft workers worried about their green cards
articles.title_zh: The advice immigration attorneys have for Microsoft workers worried about their green cards
articles.content_orig:
The Trump administration's Thursday declaration that it was suspending Microsoft and Adobe from a federal visa sponsorship program is reverberating through the tech industry.
Immigration attorneys told Business Insider that employees on H-1B visas working at Microsoft, Adobe, and the other named tech companies should seek counsel and get clarity about their status in light of the suspensions.
Individual cases may vary, and the attorneys spoke in general terms about the advice they would give without knowing a client's specific circumstances or status.
"This is a time where immigrants, high-skilled immigrants, really need to pay attention to laws," said Tahmina Watson, a business immigration attorney at Watson Immigration Law in Seattle. "Things are changing on a dime," she added.
Business Insider spoke to eight immigration attorneys on Thursday in the wake of the announcement, as part of our ongoing series, " H-1B Fallout: 1 Year Later ," which explores how foreign workers are navigating a rapidly changing US immigration landscape.
Some of the immigration attorneys said the suspensions were likely to be challenged in court. Others said they were the latest in a series of US measures targeting foreign workers. One attorney suggested they would only impact a relatively small group of workers.
"Most people will either be able to wait it out or have time to switch jobs," said Loren Locke, an attorney at Locke Immigration Law in Atlanta.
The Permanent Labor Certification, or PERM, program is an initial step that employers generally must complete before sponsoring a worker for an employment-based visa, requiring them to show that no qualified and available US workers could fill the role.
Vice President JD Vance said at a press conference on Thursday that Microsoft had "abused" this system by laying off American workers and using it to hire foreign ones, who he said were paid less. "If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants," Vance said.
Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
A Microsoft spokesperson pointed Business Insider to a blog post the company published Thursday, which said "the vast majority of Microsoft employees in the United States are Americans." The company said it pays its H-1B employees "the same as any other employees doing comparable work."
Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said at the press conference that the government would not accept any new PERM applications or process any pending ones for the named companies, which, in addition to Microsoft and Adobe, also include tech outsourcing firms Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL Technologies, and Capgemini.
In suspending new and pending PERM applications, the Trump administration left a very specific group of H-1B visa holders in limbo, said Matthew Maiona, an immigration attorney at Maiona Ward in Boston.
Maiona said that a hypothetical employee at Microsoft or Adobe, six years into an H-1B visa, could now, in theory, be ordered to appear in immigration court under this new suspension.
"You could be in trouble if you cannot qualify for another non-immigrant visa classification," Maiona said. "You may have to leave the United States."
But Locke said workers would only face potential removal if they exhausted their H-1B eligibility and could not secure an extension or another legal basis — of which there are several — to remain in the country.
Though H-1B visas have a statutory maximum of six years before expiring, they can be extended past that number if workers have made sufficient progress toward obtaining a green card, she said.
"If the goal is to crush H-1B workers, it's not great, but it's not really crushing them either," Locke said.
Todd Pomerleau, an immigration attorney based in Boston, said that with uncertainty around the extent and enforcement of the suspensions, "anybody who's concerned about their immigration status needs to seek competent counsel."
Some immigration attorneys who spoke with Business Insider said they expected the Trump administration's move to be challenged in a lawsuit that would argue the suspensions are outside the Labor Department's legal authority.
"I assume, by next week, we will start seeing lawsuits," said Kripa Upadhyay, the co-chair of Buchalter's Immigration & Global Mobility Practice, a Seattle firm.
Ted Chiappari, the head of immigration law at Duane Morris LLP, said federal statute only allows the Department of Labor to unilaterally suspend an employer from using the PERM program for 180 days.
"That gives the employer notice that there's an investigation going on, and at the end of that investigation, if they find something inappropriate, they have six years to decide whether to debar an employer," he said.
And even then, Chiappari said, they can only debar an employer for up to three years.
Few attorneys interviewed by Business Insider said they were surprised by the measure. Mostly, they saw it as another salvo in what they described as the Trump administration's ongoing crackdown on foreign workers.
Upadhyay said that just the day before, she had spoken with a Microsoft employee on an H-1B whose spouse also was on an H-1B.
The person's H-1B extension was running out, and they now faced the "impossible decision" of moving to their home country, leaving behind their spouse and two US citizen children.
"I have children to support," Upadhyay recalled the worker saying. "What happens now?"
Upadhyay expects to get more of these calls.

articles.title_orig: OLED MacBook Pro to help boost premium display shipments, per report
articles.title_zh: OLED MacBook Pro to help boost premium display shipments, per report
articles.content_orig:
A new Counterpoint Research report says Apple’s next-generation MacBook Pro will help drive a 50% increase in OLED notebook display shipments in 2026 alone. Here are the details.
In a report released today, Counterpoint Research projects that advanced notebook display shipments will grow 11% in 2026 compared to 2025, with OLED notebook display shipments expected to rise 50% for the period.
The report notes that the 11% growth in advanced notebook display shipments will comfortably outperform the broader notebook display market, which Counterpoint says it expects to decline 3% year over year.
Counterpoint says it also expects OLED to widen its lead over MiniLED in the advanced notebook display market, rising from 56% of shipments in 2025 to 75% in 2026, while MiniLED is expected to drop from 44% to 25%.
The research company says part of the growth in OLED notebook panel shipments is expected to come from Apple’s adoption of the technology in its next-generation MacBook Pro, currently rumored to be announced on October 27 with a touchscreen display and a redesigned, significantly lighter chassis.
OLED notebook display shipments are forecast to rise 50% in 2026 and another 24% in 2027. Apple’s anticipated adoption of OLED in next-generation MacBook Pro models, alongside continued demand for premium AI PCs, is expected to drive this growth.
Another factor contributing to OLED’s growth, Counterpoint says, is technology and manufacturing advances such as tandem OLED architectures, which improve brightness, power efficiency, and panel longevity.
Apple already uses tandem OLED in the iPad Pro, where two OLED layers work together to deliver higher full-screen brightness. The company is widely expected to use a similar two-stack tandem OLED architecture for the upcoming 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro models.
Looking ahead, Counterpoint expects OLED notebook panel shipments to grow at a compounded annual rate of 26% between 2024 and 2030, while panel revenue is forecast to grow at 35% per year over the same period.

articles.title_orig: Princeton Celebrates Anne Carson, a Nobel Prize Winner Who Was Denied Tenure
articles.title_zh: Princeton Celebrates Anne Carson, a Nobel Prize Winner Who Was Denied Tenure
articles.content_orig:
Anne Carson, the Canadian writer and classicist whose work blends verse, prose and essay with influences from classical myths, has won the 2026 Nobel Prize in literature for her “bold and inventive oeuvre.”
Carson, 76, is an accomplished classicist who has taught at multiple colleges in the US and Canada while also producing works like “The Beauty of the Husband,” “An Autobiography of Red: A Novel in Verse,” and “Nox.” Her distinctive essays, prose and poetry, in which the ancient and modern live side-by-side, have garnered her critical acclaim.
Carson’s “playful dialogue with the classical tradition has created new forms for contemporary literature,” the Nobel committee said in a statement.
The prize, announced at the Swedish Academy in Stockholm on Thursday, carries a cash award of 12 million Swedish kronor ($1.2 million).
Carson is widely known for hybrid style where she balances multiple ideas, genres and forms. “Almost all her literary production has centered upon the intersection between the philologist’s obsession with words and the poet’s desire for new meaning,” said Anders Olsson, chairman of the Nobel Committee for Literature.
For example, in “Autobiography of Red,” the work that made her name, her long narrative verse is framed by an erudite, enigmatic discussion of Stesichorus, the Greek poet who inspired her. In Stesichorus’ original myth, Heracles – better known by his Latin name of Hercules – kills the winged monster Geryon and steals his red cattle as one of his 12 labors. In Carson’s 1998 retelling, she recasts Geryon as a “tender ‘hero’ devoted to his mother,” who “having earlier been subjected to sexual assaults at the hands of his brother, falls in love with the smug and boorish Heracles,” the Nobel committee said.
Such a complicated form belies the simplicity of much of the language in it. “Somehow Geryon made it to adolescence.// Then he met Herakles and the kingdoms of his life all shifted down a few notches,” Carson writes. “They were two superior eels//at the bottom of the tank and they recognized each other like italics.”
Carson was in Iceland, “listening to the wind,” when she discovered she had won the Nobel Prize, according to Ingrid Carlberg, the permanent secretary of the Swedish Academy.
“She was taken by surprise but very happy – I could hear that in her voice,” Carlberg said.
Much of Carson’s early career was dominated by her work in classics – she studied for her bachelor’s, master’s and doctorate degrees at the University of Toronto and also received a diploma in classics from the University of St. Andrews in Scotland. Although she published an essay and her Ph.D. thesis in her thirties, it wasn’t until she was 42 years old that her first book of poems “Short Talks” was published. Three more works followed before “Autobiography of Red” marked her out as a critical favorite.
“The Beauty of the Husband: A Fictional Essay in 29 Tangos,” which charts the breakdown of a marriage between two unnamed characters, came three years later. For that work, Carson became the first female winner of the prestigious T.S. Eliot Prize in 2001. She is the 19th woman of the 122 individuals who have won the Nobel Prize for literature.
Nobel Prize in medicine awarded to trio for technique that helps decode mysteries of the brain
Carson is notoriously private about her personal life, but her 2010 work “Nox” reflects on the life and death of her estranged brother, Michael. It is not a traditional book, as such, but a “box containing an accordion-fold-out of picture, letters and other written texts dedicated to her dead brother,” Olsson said.
Carson has also produced several translations of classical texts and ventured into other artforms, collaborating with visual artists, choreographers, opera and theater directors. The transition into various other artistic fields “demonstrates the freedom with which she relates to literary expectations and rule systems, which in turn lies behind the outstanding importance her work since the 1990s has had for the international art and literature scene,” Olsson added.
Last year, the prize went to László Krasznahorkai “for his compelling and visionary oeuvre that, in the midst of apocalyptic terror, reaffirms the power of art,” the committee said.
In 2024, South Korean author Han Kang was honored by the committee for her “intense poetic prose that confronts historical traumas and exposes the fragility of human life.”
Literature is the fourth prize to be handed out this week, after achievements in medicine, physics and chemistry. The Nobel Peace Prize is set to be revealed on Friday, followed by the winners in economics on October 12.

articles.title_orig: Flu season didn’t start when or where it was expected. Get your shot now, health officials say
articles.title_zh: Flu season didn’t start when or where it was expected. Get your shot now, health officials say
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
This year’s flu season started months early and in an unexpected part of the country, according to health officials.
The unusually early start to the season has prompted local health officials to urge people to get their flu shots as soon as possible.
In Los Angeles County, flu activity began rising in September, ahead of its typical early-November start, Dr. Dawn Terashita told The Times on Wednesday.
That isn’t a major surprise, said Terashita, associate director of the Los Angeles County Department of Public Health’s Acute Communicable Disease Control Program. Flu tends to be “very unpredictable,” she said, due to the ways that it mutates.
But another unusual factor was that the flu season started this year in the Western states.
Typically, the flu starts in the South, then makes its way across the country, according to Dr. Elizabeth Hudson, regional chief of infectious diseases at Kaiser Permanente Southern California.
Terashita said it’s too soon to know the reason behind this phenomenon.
Given the early flu surge, Hudson said in a statment it might have caught people off-guard, as many hadn’t even had the chance to get vaccinated — or they were so recently vaccinated that their bodies hadn’t had a chance to produce immunity against the flu.
The county’s flu season started on Sept. 28. But the early start alone, Terashita noted, isn’t an indicator that the season will be more severe.
The rate at which flu tests are coming back positive since the season’s start has been high in the San Francisco Bay Area and moderate in Southern California and the Sacramento Valley. Flu hospital admission rates remain low across California. So far this year, there have been 34 flu-related deaths in the state, according to the state Department of Public Health’s online dashboard .
San Francisco confirmed its first flu death of the season last week . Los Angeles County has not logged any influenza deaths yet this season, Terashita said. In the 2025-26 flu season, the county recorded 126 influenza deaths, a relatively low total, she noted.
Kaiser has seen a recent increase in outpatient visits related to the flu, though flu hospitalizations have not yet risen. If the current trend continues, Hudson expects hospitalizations to spike in the coming weeks.
Health officials say vaccination is the best form of protection against the flu and are urging people to get their shots soon.
Dr. Peter Chin-Hong, a UC San Francisco infectious-disease expert, said people should aim to get the shot ideally before mid-October. For most, he said, the standard flu shot suffices, though he noted there are other options, including a nasal spray version — great for almost anyone with a fear of needles — and higher-dosage shots. The stronger shots have four times the antigen and are approved for those 65 and older.
The current variant, H3N2 subclade K, appears similar to last year’s strain and is included in this year’s vaccine, reducing concern about a major mismatch between the vaccine and the flu strain, Chin-Hong said.
“The ball is in our court because vaccination behavior drives how we tackle the flu,” he said. “This year we have less excuse because the flu vaccine is well-matched in general to ... what has been circulating so far.”
Los Angeles County’s most severe flu season in recent memory was the 2009 pandemic, according to Terashita. That year, the H1N1 virus led to a high number of hospitalizations and deaths around the world, The Times reported at the time.
Flu cases almost disappeared during the COVID-19 pandemic, Terashita said. As people resumed gatherings and eased up on measures including masking and social distancing, the county saw upticks in flu cases in 2024 and 2025.
“We’re just watching and waiting right now” to see how severe the flu season will be, she said, “but it is a good reminder to everyone that it’s a very good thing you can do to protect yourself, which is get the vaccine.”
Times staff writer Rong-Gong Lin contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: American Oil Refiners Are Printing Money as Wars Shrink Global Energy Supplies
articles.title_zh: American Oil Refiners Are Printing Money as Wars Shrink Global Energy Supplies
articles.content_orig:
Global refined product supply continues to tighten, pushing U.S. independent refiners toward an unprecedented earnings peak. Damage to Middle East refineries from the war, Ukraine's sustained strikes on Russian refining facilities, and reduced fuel exports from Asian countries have driven diesel and gasoline prices up far more than crude oil, positioning Valero Energy (VLO), Marathon Petroleum (MPC), and Phillips 66 (PSX) to post third-quarter earnings that could surpass their second-quarter highs across the board, with some metrics set to shatter all-time records.
According to Wall Street analyst forecasts cited by The Wall Street Journal, the three companies will report results between late October and early November. JPMorgan estimates that Valero's U.S. Gulf Coast refineries achieved an average spread of $47.11 per barrel between crude purchase prices and refined product selling prices in Q3, far above the $30.28 recorded in Q2. At that level, Valero's Q3 pre-tax profit could reach $8.95 billion, up 50% quarter-over-quarter and 24% above the quarterly record set in mid-2022.
Piper Sandler projects Marathon Petroleum's Q3 earnings per share could exceed seven times the year-ago figure; Phillips 66's refining segment profit is also expected to surpass its previous record.
Crack spreads drive profit surge
The core driver of this earnings expansion is the refining industry's key metric—the "crack spread"—the difference between crude oil purchase costs and selling prices of refined products such as diesel and gasoline. While crude prices rose in Q3, refined product prices surged even more sharply, rapidly widening the profit refiners earn per barrel processed.
The average U.S. retail diesel price recently spiked to a record $6.53 per gallon. While it has since pulled back, it remains at extremely elevated levels. South Korea's iM Securities estimates that damaged refining capacity in Russia and the Middle East alone accounts for more than 6% of total global capacity; since February, diesel export disruptions from the two regions have totaled approximately 1.6 million barrels per day.
Note: Forecasts from JPMorgan and Piper Sandler
Supply gap continues to widen
The current global refining system faces not a crude oil shortage, but a severe shortfall in processing capacity. Industrial Info Resources data shows approximately 12.1% of global refining capacity was offline as of September. Goldman Sachs estimates roughly 2 million barrels per day of refining capacity in the Middle East remains unable to operate normally.
Crude oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz have recovered significantly from the early stages of the war, but supplies of refined products—diesel, gasoline, and jet fuel—are recovering far more slowly than crude. The market is gradually resolving the question of "is there enough crude," but has yet to solve the problem of "are there enough refineries to turn crude into fuel."
The Russia-Ukraine conflict has further widened this gap. JPMorgan tallies that Ukraine has struck approximately 15 Russian refining facilities since late July, knocking close to 2 million barrels per day of refining capacity out of the market. Goldman Sachs expects that even if Brent crude falls back to around $80 per barrel, the diesel squeeze may not disappear in tandem. The bank forecasts that global diesel and jet fuel crack spreads could still average above $40 per barrel in 2027—more than double the typical level of around $20.
Dramatic re-rating of stock prices and market value
Earnings expectations are already fully reflected in the stock market. Valero, Marathon, and Phillips 66 all hit record highs on Thursday, with year-to-date gains exceeding 100% each and a combined market value increase of approximately $224 billion. Over the same period, the S&P 500 rose only about 13%. Valero's stock closed at $413 on September 18, up roughly 144% year-to-date.
Wall Street views on the outlook are diverging. UBS raised its Valero price target from $355 to $450, maintaining a "Buy" rating; Piper Sandler lifted its target from $329 to $435; Raymond James also raised its target from $350 to $450 in September. These firms broadly expect the diesel supply shortage to persist into next year, and have accordingly raised their 2027 crack spread forecasts by roughly $5 per barrel, while setting refining EBITDA expectations at 1.36 times the Wall Street average.
Morgan Stanley, while sharply raising its Valero target from $255 to $411, maintained a "Neutral" rating, arguing the current stock price already reflects much of the industry's improved fundamentals.
Why new capacity investment is absent
Such high profits have not prompted U.S. refiners to build new capacity at scale. A major refinery project requires billions of dollars in investment, and typically takes years from planning and permitting to full operation—and companies are not confident that the current high-margin environment created by war and supply disruptions will persist until a new project comes online.
U.S. refining capacity has generally declined over the past decade. Data shows U.S. refining capacity peaked at approximately 18.6 million barrels per day in 2017, fell to 17.6 million barrels per day by 2025, and is expected to decline further to roughly 17.45 million barrels per day this year.
The U.S. government has recently convened refiners to discuss expanding domestic refining capacity. The Trump administration and industry figures have also discussed restarting two recently closed California refineries—Phillips 66's Los Angeles-area facility and Valero's Benicia refinery. The two facilities previously accounted for roughly 20% of California's refining capacity combined. But restarting them also faces equipment, logistics, and crude supply challenges; even if companies decide to resume production, it could take months.
John Auers, refined products analyst at Novi Labs, believes global refining capacity is currently "extremely tight," and U.S. refiners could maintain elevated profitability through 2027, but companies are still unlikely to launch major new construction projects because the industry broadly views the current environment as abnormal.
Valero's competitive advantage also extends to crude procurement costs. More than 60% of the company's U.S. refining capacity is concentrated on the Gulf Coast, compared with 42% for Marathon Petroleum and 27% for Phillips 66. The Gulf Coast is the hub of major U.S. pipelines and import/export terminals, offering relatively convenient access to crude from the U.S., Canada, Venezuela, and Central and South America. iM Securities analysis notes that in Q1, Valero increased its use of Canadian crude—up to $26 per barrel cheaper than WTI—and resumed Venezuelan crude imports, with this procurement optimization contributing roughly 30% of the refining segment's incremental profit for the quarter.
Valero returned $2.6 billion to shareholders in Q2, equivalent to 59% of adjusted operating cash flow. As of end-June, the company held $7.9 billion in cash and cash equivalents, above the $4 billion to $5 billion range it considers appropriate. The company has not cut its dividend since 2012 and has consistently repurchased shares, with shares outstanding last year down 27% from 2021. Its medium-to-long-term policy is to return more than 50% of EBITDA to shareholders.
Market participants caution that the current high-margin environment carries multiple risk variables. Hurricanes could force Gulf Coast refinery shutdowns, and changes in Venezuelan crude policy could affect feedstock supply. Once crack spreads normalize, refining earnings will inevitably retreat from their current abnormally elevated levels.

articles.title_orig: ‘You’ve Hired Half the Third Reich’: 6 Key Moments From the Georgia Senate Debate
articles.title_zh: ‘You’ve Hired Half the Third Reich’: 6 Key Moments From the Georgia Senate Debate
articles.content_orig:
Candidates traded personal attacks and clashed over a range of issues in closely watched US Senate debates on Thursday, with control of Congress at stake
With just weeks left in the contentious midterm election campaign, candidates in a trio of highly-competitive Senate races debated Thursday night, clashing over the economy, tariffs, the Iran war and abortion rights, with control of the upper chamber at stake.
In Georgia, incumbent Democratic senator Jon Ossoff faced GOP representative Mike Collins. In Michigan, Democrat Abdul Al-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers debated over the state’s open Senate seat. And in Maine, longtime senator Susan Collins met Democratic challenger Troy Jackson. Democrats need to flip four Republican-held Senate seats to win the majority.
Here are the key takeaways from the battleground state debates.
Affordability was a major topic across all three debates on Thursday night, as voters consistently name the cost of goods, gas, housing and healthcare as their top concerns in this year’s midterms.
“Can you afford your gas? Can you afford your groceries under this guy who’s going to rubber stamp everything Donald Trump tells him to rubber stamp?” El-Sayed asked during the Michigan debate, the first of two in one of this cycle’s most fiercely contested races.
Both Rogers and El-Sayed said they support suspending a fuel tax to alleviate costs, while El-Sayed argued that the Iran war, which was driving up gas prices, needs to end. El-Sayed attacked Rogers for growing his personal wealth while in office as a US representative.
Rogers called El-Sayed “bought off” by billionaire George Soros, Hamas and Hezbollah. “We cannot afford Abdul, and we cannot risk his ideology,” Rogers said.
In Georgia, Ossoff repeatedly asked Collins to justify his support for Trump’s global tariff policies, which the senator said have “crushed Georgia families” and “strangled” economic growth.
“Let’s see if he has the courage to explain his votes,” Ossoff said, adding later: “Still have not heard an explanation for the tariffs.”
Collins, who is trying to cut into Ossoff’s lead, blamed inflation on Biden administration policies, singling out spending measures that his opponent had supported.
Later in Maine, where polls show a tight race, Jackson focused his remarks on pocketbook issues, including the sharp spike in heating oil costs and high energy prices.
Collins defended her record and argued that Maine had benefited from the $50bn rural health transformation fund that was appended to Trump’s signature tax cut and spending bill, the so-called Big Beautiful bill.
In the Georgia debate, a question about data centers erupted into a pointed, personal exchange between Ossoff and Collins.
“Mike Collins voted to take that money out of your pocket and out of your community and give it instead to data center developers,” Ossoff said.
He then accused Collins of being a “bigot” who has “hired half the Third Reich” – a reference to the congressman’s history of employing staffers who have expressed white nationalist, antisemitic, and extremist views online.
“If John Lewis were marching today from Selma to Montgomery,” Ossoff said of the late civil rights icon and long-serving Georgia congressman, “Mike Collins would be grabbing a billy club. His office has been in cahoots with some of the most notorious white supremacists on the country.”
Collins was asked directly about his son-in-law’s social media posts promoting white nationalist and antisemitic views.
“You know, Rick, that’s my family,” Collins replied. “That’s the craziness that Jon Ossoff has been spewing out there.” Collins noted that a New York man had recently been charged after threatening to kill him, and added: “I’ve condemned racism, antisemitism, hate; I don’t care where the source is. And I tell him that too, it’s wrong. We have no place in this world for that.”
Collins, meanwhile, sought to cast Ossoff as “radical” and an “extremist” whose record in the Senate had left the state “less safe, more expensive and worse off”.
Tariffs were also a topic of heated debate in Michigan, which shares hundreds of miles of border with Canada.
This week, Rogers publicly backtracked on previous support for Trump’s tariffs on the US’s northern neighbor , saying in a campaign ad that “Canada is not our enemy” and that the “tariff war” needed to end now.
During Thursday night’s debate, Rogers said he had spoken to the commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, this week to advocate for a deal between the two countries. There are tariffs in place that are “too high and not helpful for us”, Rogers said.
El-Sayed said he supports targeted, logical tariffs that protect Michigan manufacturing, but nothing like the “ham-fisted, chaotic, self-serving” tariffs Trump put in place. He called out Rogers for “flip-flopping” on the issue, saying he was only reversing his stance because of “sagging poll numbers”.
“He’s doing an ad drinking a Labatt and talking about the Red Wings, pretending like he was not for this the entire time,” El-Sayed said. “Be serious, my guy.”
In Maine, discussions about gas prices and the war in Iran raised notable tension in the second debate between Jackson and Collins, who is seeking a sixth term in her seat. “She’s the Chairman of Appropriations,” Jackson said. “Money has to come through them for these wars – she still can do something.”
Collins, who plans to continue leading the Appropriations committee if re-elected, said she had repeatedly supported war powers resolutions to halt Trump’s military action in Iran.
But Jackson pushed further, accusing the senator and her husband of profiting from the war.
She could use her leverage to stop this war, but instead they’re making money,” he said, prompting a furious response from Collins, who called the allegation “absolutely outrageous”.
“You owe me an apology,” she said.
In Maine, both candidates were also pressed to address inconsistencies in their positions on reproductive rights, a crucial issue for voters in the state.
“Our records have changed,” Jackson said. “Mine has gotten better – hers has gotten worse.”
He pointed to Collins’ vote to confirm supreme court justice Brett Kavanaugh, who helped overturn Roe v Wade in 2022 . Collins, one of just two Republican senators who supports abortion rights, has said she does not regret her vote for Kavanaugh, even though she believed he had given her private assurances before his 2018 confirmation that he would not overturn the landmark ruling. Collins sought to turn the issue back on her opponent, noting his past stances on abortion that have left many voters wary. “From 2000 until he ran for the house seat in 2013 was very anti-choice,” she said, accusing Jackson of having held “extremist” views on abortion. “He was for a bill that would not allow abortion when the mother’s life was at risk.” She also pointed to legislation she helped write that sought to “codify Roe v Wade nationwide,” but the bill never made it passed the Senate.
In Michigan, Rogers repeatedly attacked El-Sayed by attempting to tie him to Muslim terrorist groups, including Hamas, and suggested government surveillance would only bother someone if he or his family had something to hide.
Rogers brought up El-Sayed’s mom and sister, prompting El-Sayed to say at one point that Rogers should just come out and say what he’s been dancing around all night, after Rogers’ repeated references to terrorist groups.
“He wants this to be about anything but his own record,” El-Sayed said.
Rogers claimed El-Sayed refused to condemn a terrorist attack in Michigan earlier this year and the 7 October Hamas terrorist attacks in Gaza, although El-Sayed said he had condemned both.
But, El-Sayed added: “I’m not somebody who tries to make political theater out of other people’s pain.”
He also retorted to Rogers: “Did you sell your yachts?” Rogers responded: “I never owned a yacht in Florida, brother.”

articles.title_orig: World Octopus Day: new discoveries about the world’s smartest invertebrates
articles.title_zh: World Octopus Day: new discoveries about the world’s smartest invertebrates
articles.content_orig:
If you liked this story, share it with other people.
Happy World Octopus Day!  Every Oct 8, the world celebrates one of the more unusual creatures of the sea. Octopuses are well-known for their eight legs and ability to squirt ink when frightened. They’ve also been known to use tools, a sign of intelligence, and can shape-shift to mimic the colors and texture of their surroundings, an effective way to disappear from both predators and prey.
Mongabay has reported on several octopus discoveries this year, including:
Ancient octopus were apex predators
Modern colossal squid are believed to be the largest invertebrates in the sea, but Mongabay’s Shanna Hanbury recently reported on an even larger ancient octopus species whose fossils were described by Japanese researchers in April 2026.
The Japanese team found a fossilized jawbone from the now-extinct Nanaimoteuthis haggarti. Based on its jaw size, researchers suggest the octopus may have reached 6.6 to 18.6 meters (22 to 61 feet) in length. On the higher end, that’s around two-thirds the size of an adult blue whale, the largest animal to ever exist.
“It suggests that it may have been among the largest invertebrates ever known,” study co-author Yasuhiro Iba, a paleontologist at Hokkaido University in Japan, told Mongabay by email.
They were likely gigantic predators that roamed the late Cretaceous seas between 100 million to 72 million years ago.
A rare look at baby octopuses
From long dead octopus to newly born, Hanbury also reported on baby Argentine octopuses and a rare photo of them.
Patagonian octopus eggs in Puerto Lobos Protected Natural Area in Argentina. Image courtesy of Martin Brogger.
These eggs belong to a small Patagonian octopus ( Octopus tehuelchus ). It’s one of the more common octopus species in the region, but researchers still haven’t been able to determine its global conservation status, although reported catches in Patagonia have declined over the past 50 years.
The black dots inside each egg are the developing eyes of the embryos, indicating that they’re progressing toward hatching. The female octopus of this species often lays her eggs in the shell of an oyster , then guards them fiercely. She even stops eating during this period.
New octopus species are described often , including a blue octopus about the size of a golf ball recently discovered in the Galapagos.
On a deep-sea expedition in 2015, scientists used a remotely operated vehicle to find a golf-ball sized, short-armed blue octopus. In a recent study , they confirmed that it’s new to science, reported Mongabay’s David Brown.
However, questions remain about how the new species, Microeledone galapagensis , makes use of its stubby arms.
“If you gather prey by moving your arms through the sediment (as we think they do), wouldn’t it be better to have longer arms with more suckers than short little arms?” queried lead author Janet Voight.
Banner image: Big blue octopus ( Octopus cyanea ) with a diver in background. Image courtesy of David Fleetham/WWF via naturepl.com.

articles.title_orig: 4 astronauts return to Earth after 8 months in space
articles.title_zh: 4 astronauts return to Earth after 8 months in space
articles.content_orig:
CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. — Four astronauts returned to Earth from the International Space Station on Thursday after hurrying there eight months ago to replace an ailing colleague and his crew.
SpaceX brought the U.S., French and Russian flyers back with a splashdown in the Pacific off the coast of Los Angeles.
NASA's Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway, France's Sophie Adenot and Russia's Andrey Fedyaev departed the orbiting lab on Wednesday, eager to reunite with their families after a lengthy separation. Their replacements arrived three weeks late because of capsule repairs, stalling this crew's homecoming.
They couldn't wait to feel the breeze on their faces, hit the shower and, for Adenot at least, plunge back into water sports.
"We are so excited to be back on Planet Earth after an incredible mission on the International Space Station," Meir radioed moments after splashing down. While still in orbit, she said the crew had "a lot of mixed, swirling emotions" and would miss the "extraordinary views of our home planet."
All four were out of their capsule within an hour, waving and pumping their fists in the air aboard SpaceX's recovery ship. After a helicopter ride to shore, they were going to head for Houston.
Meir and her crew left the planet in February to replace four station occupants who were sent home early after one of them — NASA's Mike Fincke, now retired — fell ill . It was NASA's first medical evacuation in 65 years of human spaceflight.
The new foursome watched with pride two months later as the Artemis II astronauts flew around the moon. They also celebrated the United States' 250th birthday up there, with Meir joining the Boston Pops with her piccolo for a Fourth of July concert.
Meir took part in four spacewalks, while Adenot ventured outside three times for maintenance and upgrades to the 28-year-old outpost.
In the middle of all the work, the astronauts found time for fun, throwing a dance party last month and holding regular cooking demonstrations complete with aprons and a chef's toque.
Meir presented a how-to video for curly-haired spacewomen like herself, while Hathaway kept his bushy mustache — a space rarity — groomed to perfection. He grew the naval aviator-style mustache before rocketing into orbit as a way to honor his Navy ties, and found it no harder to maintain in weightlessness than on Earth. Some ground controllers grew mustaches in solidarity.
Will his mustache disappear now that his mission is over?
"It's kind of become a little bit of my brand up here," Hathaway said in August, "so I don't know if it'll go away right away or I'll end up keeping it for a while."
Seven astronauts remain aboard the space station, representing the U.S., Russia and Canada. The outpost has welcomed 298 visitors from 26 countries since the doors swung open in 2000, by NASA's count.

But it usually took a year or more before those lessons showed up publicly in People’s Liberation Army (PLA) training, equipment or force structure, Lilly Min-Chen Lee and Kateryna Bondar wrote in a commentary published on October 7 by the Washington-based Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS).

articles.title_orig: ESPN’s ‘College GameDay’ makes major decision as Hurricane Isaias looms
articles.title_zh: ESPN’s ‘College GameDay’ makes major decision as Hurricane Isaias looms
articles.content_orig:
ESPN’s “College GameDay” is moving indoors on Saturday.
The upcoming rendition of the college football pregame show set to take place at Alabama is forced to stray away from its traditional outdoor programming due to the impending hurricane expected to slam the area in the coming days.
Hurricane Isaias, which was upgraded to a Category 2 storm Thursday evening, is on a direct path to make landfall on the coasts of Florida, Alabama and Mississippi and is expected to bring extreme weather to the area.
To prepare for the storms, “GameDay” will be hosted inside Coleman Coliseum on Alabama’s campus, and the show is expected to run as usual, according to an announcement from ESPN .
This is not the first time ESPN has been forced to move its flagship college football program indoors this season, with “GameDay” having to temporarily relocate to LSU’s student union in Week 1 because of nearby lightning strikes.
As for Saturday’s SEC matchup between Alabama and Georgia, the game is still on for 7:30 p.m. ET, but the impending hurricane could affect that.
Amid the storms, officials from both Alabama and the SEC say that the hurricane will be closely monitored throughout the upcoming days.
“Alabama athletics continues to closely monitor the weather forecast ahead of Saturday’s football game, with the safety and well-being of the student-athletes, coaches, staff and fans as our highest priority,” the university said in a statement Wednesday night . “We remain in close communication with the National Weather Service, the Southeastern Conference office and the University of Georgia as we observe conditions.
“At this time, kickoff remains scheduled for 6:30 p.m. CT on Saturday. We continue to encourage fans to rely on official Alabama athletics and SEC channels for the latest information regarding Saturday’s game.”

articles.title_orig: Microsoft Suspended From Green Card Program as Trump Officials Widen Fraud Drive
articles.title_zh: Microsoft Suspended From Green Card Program as Trump Officials Widen Fraud Drive
articles.content_orig:
Vance singled out Microsoft, accusing the company of fraud.
Vice President JD Vance on Thursday announced the suspension of tech giants, Microsoft and Adobe, from a green card program -- effectively blocking the companies from sponsoring H-1B visa workers for permanent residency green cards.
The suspension is from the PERM program -- a certification that allows employers to hire a foreign employee to work permanently in the U.S.
Vance singled out Microsoft, accusing the company of fraud.
"So if the H-1B visa is how the people get into the country, the PERM program is how they stay in the United States to begin with," Vance said. "Now there has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused the system more than Microsoft."
In a statement to ABC News, Microsoft said it "succeeds as a global technology leader by developing the world’s best technology workforce. We do this by strengthening this country’s talent pipeline, hiring American workers, and attracting the best talent from around the world."
Critics of the PERM program have said it allows companies to recruit foreign workers, taking away jobs from Americans. Vance alleged Microsoft employees were laid off -- later replaced by "foreign indentured servants" who "are earning wages that are far below the average for American citizens."
"So, in the last year, Microsoft -- and I want to be clear about the data here, so let me check this -- but Microsoft laid off last year 6,000 American workers," Vance said. "At the same time, the company benefited from 6,300 H-1B visas and almost 3,000 green cards."
"In other words, if you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants."
Microsoft said in a statement that "the vast majority of Microsoft employees in the United States are Americans."
It also pushed back on Vance's comments, saying it "only files H-1B petitions for those who meet the rigorous standards of this visa category."
"We pay our employees some of the highest compensation in the tech sector, and our wages are among the highest of all H-1B filings. We pay our H-1B employees the same as any other employees doing comparable work," the statement continued.
The criticism of Microsoft came hours before President Donald Trump awarded Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella the Medal of Technology and Innovation during an event at the Institute of Peace on Thursday.
Trump lauded Nadella at the ceremony, saying he has been "a key figure in the transformation of Microsoft, revolutionizing the company and empowering businesses, students and consumers from all over the world with some of the most capable software ever built or ever even conceived."
Vance acknowledged the contradiction of honoring Microsoft's CEO the same day as his announcement.
"Microsoft is a great American company, and we have a great relationship with them. They do a lot of important things," Vance said. "So we're going to continue to support Microsoft and have a great relationship with Microsoft, but we're also going to deny them the ability to apply for these permanent residencies until they show that they are going to get serious about putting American workers first."
ABC News has reached out to Adobe for comment.
Asked how long the suspension will be in place, Vance said it will "last as long as it needs to" and added that the administration has "a number of tools to suspend it indefinitely" if needed.
Vance, who has been asked to lead the administration’s Anti-Fraud Task Force, also criticized the H-1B visa program as a whole, saying it has become "rife with fraud" in recent years.
"The H-1B visa program is meant to allow companies to bring in really the best of the best from outside the United States of America for positions that are completely impossible to fill with American workers. Unfortunately, the program has become rife with fraud over the last several years, probably the last several decades," Vance said.
Attorney General Todd Blanche also chimed in about the issue of "foreign labor favoritism," promising that companies will be investigated if they "discriminate against an American worker in favor of someone on the other side of the world," with Blanche saying this "violate[s] the trust of the federal government and the American people."
"The Department of Justice, my department, is actively investigating companies that do this that favor foreign workers over the American people,” Blanche said.
Inspector General of Labor Anthony D'Esposito also announced that the Department of Labor is conducting a "historic investigation into the J-1 visa fraud involving nine major American universities: Pitt, Yale, Harvard, Stanford, Brown, UC Davis, CaltTech, Arizona State, and MIT," with investigations already underway, he said.
"If an American university is breaking the law to save a dollar, while exposing American research to a foreign adversary, that is not academic excellence. It's institutional betrayal," D'Esposito said.

articles.title_orig: Open Door Mission hosts 24-hour 'Conversations on a Bench' for World Homeless Day
articles.title_zh: Open Door Mission hosts 24-hour 'Conversations on a Bench' for World Homeless Day
articles.content_orig:
Rochester, N.Y. — This Saturday will mark World Homeless Day, and the Open Door Mission is raising awareness.
Thursday, it's participating in "Conversations on a Bench", a 24-hour livestream event.
Ministry CEO’s will spend 24 hours sitting on a bench engaging in conversations with anyone who stops by.
The idea is to re-humanize homelessness and amplify stories of hope and transformation.
"There are many, many reasons why homelessness comes about," said Open Door Mission CEO Robert Williams. "Here in Rochester, two of the primary drivers are addiction and mental illness."
He added, "I am celebrating 19 years of recovery. I went through a 25-year addiction. So I walked that path, and I sit here now as the CEO of the open door mission because there was something that was called hope."
The conversations continue at the corner of Plymouth Avenue and Main Street through 3 p.m. Friday.

articles.title_orig: The long-deployed USS Lincoln returns home to San Diego Bay
articles.title_zh: The long-deployed USS Lincoln returns home to San Diego Bay
articles.content_orig:
Sailors wave aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier as it returns to Naval Air Station North Island after deployment Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026, in Coronado, Calif. Gregory Bull/AP hide caption
CORONADO, Calif. — After more than 10 months at sea, thousands of sailors Thursday poured out of the the USS Lincoln on San Diego Bay to thunderous cheers, streaming tears and emotional hugs, marking a homecoming that included new dads who met babies born while they were away on a historic deployment supporting the Iran war.
The reunion followed an emotional rollercoaster for families who described crying and losing sleep after hearing reports of supply shortages and deteriorating mental health among the crew during the deployment that spent a record 265 days of uninterrupted time at sea. Many said they only could communicate with family via the occasional email or rare WhatsApp calls.
Abel Ramirez, 20, was glad to have that all behind him. He walked off the carrier with a big grin, overjoyed that his first deployment was over.
"It feels amazing," he said while headed out to search for his parents who traveled from Texas. "There was a certain point when I never thought I would come off."
Cassity Garduque, 14, waved as her mom in her sailor uniform frantically waved back from the top deck after the ship docked at the pier.
"It feels really overwhelming," she said about being seeing her mom again. "She missed most of my seventh grade and my birthday."
She added that she's happy her mom won't be eating ramen almost every day and can celebrate with her now.
Family and friends cheer as the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier returns to Naval Air Station North Island after deployment Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026, in Coronado, Calif. Gregory Bull/AP hide caption
Capt. Daniel Keeler, the ship's commander, said most of the crew was on their first deployment and that the issues they faced were normal for such a long deployment, adding everyone had access to four meals a day.
"It's a floating city as you can see and at any moment there might be a clogged toilet," he said.
The Navy initially downplayed any problems during the deployment, and President Donald Trump commented in August that the Lincoln's lengthy deployment was "not nearly long enough."
Navy leaders eventually acknowledged there were some issues aboard.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth flew out to the Lincoln on Wednesday to give the crew the Presidential Unit Citation, the highest honor a unit can receive.
Hegseth told the crew that "what makes the U.S. military and the U.S. Navy and all these sailors different is that you adapt and that you're resilient and you overcome — you finish the mission nonetheless."
Hegseth pushed back against what he said were efforts to turn the "Lincoln into some sort of a symbol, a symbol of dysfunction or a symbol of low morale or a symbol of a failed mission."
The USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier returns to the San Diego Bay after deployment Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026, in San Diego. Jae C. Hong/AP hide caption
The Lincoln, which set a record for uninterrupted time at sea, is the second carrier to endure an unusually long deployment during the Iran war and to receive the Presidential Unit Citation afterward, typically reserved for significant achievement in combat.
The crew of the USS Gerald R. Ford returned in May from a 326-day deployment — the longest for an aircraft carrier in the past 50 years and a record in the post-Vietnam War era. The Lincoln's deployment of 322 days was just shy of that.
Among the first to depart the carrier at the naval base in Coronado were 64 fathers meeting their babies for the first time, the Navy said. With the airwing included, there were 122 new dads, Keeler said.
Waiting for the Lincoln to bring her husband home, sailor Kathy Monterrosa held her 6-month-old daughter, Sarahi, outfitted in a tiny blue and white sailor dress.
"She's our deployment baby," said Monterrosa, of Virginia Beach, Virginia.
It was tough to hear about the ship's conditions while she was pregnant, she said. "I was crying a lot and worried. I wasn't sure if he was OK or not," she said.
When she finally heard from her husband, he told her it was "pretty bad," but now she said she feels blessed to have her family home.
Sailor Steven Rivas beamed as he held is 7-month-old daughter.
"I couldn't grasp the reality of it," he said about coming home. He became overwhelmed as they pulled into the bay, "seeing everyone and knowing my family was waiting for me," Rivas said, his voice shaking as his eyes teared up.
The USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier returns to the San Diego Bay after deployment Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026, in San Diego. Karl Anderson/AP hide caption
Alma Solano Velez said her husband gave his family an extensive list of the foods he has been craving over the past 10 months: oxtail, barbecue chicken, broccoli and shrimp empanadas to name a few.
He had told his wife about "the lack of food and showers" on board and was looking forward to seeing their daughter, who turned 4 while he was away, she said.
The carrier left San Diego in November and arrived in the Middle East in January. U.S. and Israeli forces launched airstrikes against Iran on Feb. 28.
In August, acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said the Lincoln maintained adequate food supplies, but because combat operations limited resupply opportunities, meal options were reduced for a short time.
After more than 10 months at sea, the Lincoln's crew got a stop in Thailand early last month on the way back from the Middle East.
Extended naval deployments can wear on service members who are away from home for long periods and increase strain on the ship and its equipment.
The Navy told lawmakers that eight sailors attempted suicide during the record-setting deployment, though experts say that number is low in a strike group of 6,000 sailors over 10 months.
According to the citation that Hegseth read to the crew, the Lincoln and its strike group executed nearly 3,700 combat missions, launched 450 Tomahawk cruise missiles, shot down 77 one-way attack drones, sank 64 Iranian warships, and destroyed 21 anti-ship cruise missiles.
Another carrier, the usually Asia-based USS George Washington, relieved the Lincoln in the Middle East in August.

articles.title_orig: Dell launches Nvidia RTX Spark laptop with 18-core CPU, 3.2K 120Hz OLED display and 99 Wh battery
articles.title_zh: Dell launches Nvidia RTX Spark laptop with 18-core CPU, 3.2K 120Hz OLED display and 99 Wh battery
articles.content_orig:
The XPS 16 Creator Edition brings Nvidia’s RTX Spark platform to Dell’s XPS lineup. It joins other RTX Spark laptops such as the Asus ProArt P16 and is aimed at creative work and local AI tasks.
We previously covered the XPS 16 Creator Edition when Dell first revealed the RTX Spark-powered laptop at Computex 2026. The company has now confirmed its retail configuration, pricing and availability.
The XPS 16 Creator Edition uses an 18-core Nvidia N1X chip with 5,120 GPU cores, along with 32 GB of unified LPDDR5X memory and a 512 GB PCIe SSD. Nvidia's RTX Spark platform scales up to 20 CPU cores, 6,144 GPU cores and 128 GB of unified memory.
It comes with a 16-inch 3.2K Tandem OLED touchscreen. It has a 3,200 x 2,000 resolution and a variable refresh rate of up to 120 Hz. The screen supports HDR True Black 600, covers the full DCI-P3 color range and has a Delta E below 2. Dell also says it is Pantone Verified.
The laptop is 17.8 mm thick and weighs about 2.02 kg (4.45 lb). Dell uses an aluminum body made with CNC machining, along with a glass touchpad.
Port selection includes three USB4 ports with DisplayPort 2.1 and Power Delivery, along with HDMI 2.1b, a full-size SDXC v7.1 card reader and a 3.5 mm audio jack. On the wireless side, the XPS 16 supports Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6.0.
Like other RTX Spark laptops , the XPS 16 uses a unified memory architecture that allows the CPU and GPU to access the same memory pool. This setup can benefit workloads that require large amounts of data to be shared between the processor and graphics hardware.
The XPS 16 is also entering the market alongside other RTX Spark creator laptops, including the Asus ProArt P16 , MSI Prestige N16 Flip AI . Asus has already launched its 16-inch model globally with up to a 20-core Grace CPU, 6,144-core Blackwell GPU, 128 GB of unified memory and 2 TB of storage.
The XPS 16 is slightly heavier than the 1.77 kg (3.9 lb) ProArt P16. Dell's 99 Wh battery is also slightly smaller than the ProArt P16's 99.9 Wh unit.
Compared with the Asus ProArt P16, Dell's panel has a lower maximum resolution and HDR brightness. The Asus model offers a 3,840 x 2,400 OLED display with up to 1,600 nits HDR brightness.
The Dell XPS 16 Creator Edition is currently available for pre-order at Best Buy for $3,799.99, with the first units expected to arrive on October 16. Dell says it will also sell the laptop through its own website. The Asus ProArt P16 starts at $2,799.99 in the US, making it $1,000 cheaper than the XPS 16.
The listed XPS 16 configuration comes with 32 GB of unified memory and 512 GB of SSD storage. Dell has not yet published pricing for the higher-spec configurations or other regions.

articles.title_orig: World’s largest wildlife crossing is on track to open this winter — unless El Niño intervenes
articles.title_zh: World’s largest wildlife crossing is on track to open this winter — unless El Niño intervenes
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
The world’s largest wildlife crossing over the 101 Freeway in Agoura Hills is barreling toward a Dec. 2 completion date . Perhaps the only thing that could stop it is a fierce winter storm.
Already, a concrete bridge stretches across 10 lanes of whizzing traffic. Atop that, there’s a lush landscape sewn with 6,000 native plants. Recently, crews completed another overpass over adjacent Agoura Road. A big remaining to-do is to fill in the gap between the freeway and the road — and the freeway to the land to the north — with millions of cubic feet of soil to create a seamless pathway for animals.
The idea behind the Wallis Annenberg Wildlife Crossing is to provide a lifeline for mountain lions in the Santa Monica Mountains, locked in by traffic and suffering from the effects of inbreeding.
“We’re just hoping El Niño ‘s on our side,” said Beth Pratt, president of the Wildlife Crossing Fund and public face of the project. “I keep saying, ‘Mother Nature, we’re trying to help you. Let’s not throw any more complications our way.’” A super-sized version of the climate pattern is looming, and there’s a good chance Southern California could be doused.
Some rain is not a big deal but flooding would shut down work for safety reasons. At a final construction update held near the crossing Thursday, Robert Rock, lead landscape architect and principal designer for the crossing, explained that the soil in the area is rich in clay and silt. When wet, it gets dangerously slick and slippery.
Heavy precipitation can also derail the soil compaction process, where crews lay down the soil in layers and go over each with a construction vehicle known as a roller. In the distance, workers were busy doing just that as the fierce late morning sun beat down.
“If you’re trying to compact a mud puddle, it wouldn’t really compact, right?” he said at a trailhead off of Agoura Road. “Because if you push that down, the mud just [splats] in either direction.”
In fact, something like that happened amid historic rains in the winter of 2022-23. Construction workers were busy preparing to pour the concrete for the bottom layer of the north wall. But water collected in the trench that was dug for it as they were working to compact the soil.
That pushed back the original completion date of late 2025. Right-wing pundits and politicos in recent months have attacked the project over the delays and a high price tag that’s currently $114 million. A March post in an outlet published by a conservative think tank called it a “bridge to nowhere” and “jobs program for environmentalists.” U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy compared it with the state’s long-delayed, budget-busting high-speed train.
Around the time the outrage reached a fever pitch, however, the completion date was announced.
Pratt said “the hate” has worn on her. She’s been called a “fraud,” “retard” and worse, and she’s even afraid to post about the crossing on social media. “Of course we’re still going to celebrate” at the finish line, she said.
At stake is the survival of the Santa Monica Mountains’ isolated, beleaguered mountain lion population, which is listed as threatened. Seth Riley, wildlife branch chief for the Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area, said 41% of documented matings were between close relatives since 2002, the start of an ongoing study of mountain lions in and around the Santa Monicas.
Just a few months ago, the National Park Service caught a young collared male at the western end of the mountain range who had a kinked tail — a sign of inbreeding. It’s not the first such documented deformity but shows the problems persist, Riley said. If the situation gets to the point where their reproduction is affected, modeling has shown there’s “essentially a 100% chance of extinction” within 50 years, he added.
But he doesn’t think it’s too late. The soon-to-open crossing will let the big cats seek mates in the Simi Hills and beyond — and allow fresh blood to travel into their neck of the woods, he said. Genetic diversity is expected to go up, though not overnight.
In the last three weeks, a trail camera stationed close to the south end of the crossing has captured coyotes, deer, a female lion with two big cubs — even as construction churns on next door, said Jeff Sikich, a wildlife biologist at the Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area.
Recently, in the Simi Hills north of the crossing, his team marked three kittens, the first litter for the 3 ½-year-old lion known as P-113.
“These kittens might be — once they grow up and leave mom at roughly around 1½ — one of the first lions to actually use the wildlife crossing,” he said.

Since joining The Times in 2020, she has investigated mental health policy and jumped on breaking news. Reggie Bush was the face of USC football’s glory years — and one of the figures at the center of its collapse. articles.title_zh: Flavio Bolsonaro says he would work with China and US as Brazil’s president
articles.content_orig:
As leader, Bolsonaro would assume control of an economy that is heavily dependent on China – by far Brazil’s largest trading partner
Flavio Bolsonaro said he would work with the US and China if he becomes Brazil’s president, after a surprise election performance left him poised to join a wave of conservative leaders pushing Latin America closer to Washington.
Bolsonaro finished ahead of President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva by about two points in Sunday’s first-round election, a result that sparked a surge in Brazilian assets due to investor views that he is more likely to pursue market-friendly financial policies.
Bolsonaro would take 52 per cent to Lula’s 48 per cent of valid votes, excluding blank and invalid ballots, in the October 25 run-off, a Datafolha poll released on Thursday evening showed. The survey has a margin of error of plus or minus two percentage points. Bolsonaro outperformed Datafolha’s final poll of the first round by about five points.
